name: Colin Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Colin. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say is confidential. Would you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Helen and I farm Greystones: 250 sows indoors, so we breed and finish pigs, and 260 hectares of wheat and field beans that mostly go back into the pig feed. I'm in the farrowing house at six, checking the new litters, then a quick meeting with Stuart, our unit manager, and the two apprentices. After that it's whatever's pressing: the feed mill, a sick pen, or the beans if it's harvest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned apprentices. Tell me more about that.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We take two a year from the agricultural college. I've trained twenty-six over the years, and nine of them run farms now. That's what I'm proudest of, more than any pig price. A good apprentice learns to read a pen before he reads a screen, and then he can do both.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about technology, and life outside the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm not first, but I'm not last. Tom, my son-in-law, works in computers and he showed me one of these AI chat tools, so I use it now and then to check feed prices or write a letter to the bank. I'm an elder at the chapel, Helen keeps the books and the holiday cottages we rent out, and our three are grown: Ben builds houses, Kate teaches and Emily's a nurse. We're comfortable: no debt, two cottages, savings. I'm fifty-eight and I'd thought I'd go till sixty-five, maybe sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that sounds sensible. Most new things end up like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are handy but they don't feed a pig. To the apprentices I'd say keep learning the basics, because the basics don't go out of fashion. Online, nothing, I don't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately the same, more or less. It means Greystones goes on as it is, the apprentices still have farms to go to, and I hand over in my own time. I'd be a little sorry, because Tom was sure it'd make the paperwork vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep taking two apprentices a year, keep using the chat tool for letters, keep the plan to retire at sixty-five. Maybe I'd let Stuart buy one of the camera systems that weigh pigs, around eight thousand, once a couple of the bigger units said it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the chapel on an ordinary Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the basics don't go out of fashion. What's the most important basic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching. A pig tells you she's ill two days before she shows it, if you watch. Ears, the way she lies, whether she gets up for feed. I make the apprentices stand in a pen for ten minutes without touching anything in their first week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone on the farm be disappointed by this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom, if he counts. And Stuart a bit, he likes the new kit. The apprentices wouldn't notice, they've enough to learn without it.

S0.say: I'd say the tools are handy but they don't feed a pig. I'd tell the apprentices to keep learning the basics, because those don't go out of fashion.
S0.think: It means the farm goes on, the apprentices still have farms to go to, and I hand over in my own time. I'd be a little sorry the paperwork didn't vanish as my son-in-law promised.
S0.do: Carries on taking two apprentices a year and using the chat tool for letters, retiring at sixty-five as planned. May let his unit manager buy an eight-thousand camera weighing system once bigger units vouch for it.
S0.feel: Calm, like chapel on an ordinary Sunday.
S0.quote: I make the apprentices stand in a pen for ten minutes without touching anything in their first week.
S0.fieldNote: Colin measures his life by the apprentices he has trained, nine of whom now run farms. He adopts proven kit after bigger units vouch for it. His teaching method of standing still and watching says a lot about his values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right, if I had to guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses that adapt will do well, and that's how it's always been. To the college I'd say teach the young ones to run the machines as well as the pigs. I'm not one for asking government to fix it, the industry should train its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think it's fine for Greystones, we're big enough to buy what works. What worries me is the apprentices: if farms need fewer people, where do my lads and lasses go? I've always been able to ring a friend and find them a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for a year or two, then buy what the bigger units had proven: probably automatic feeders and the camera weighing, maybe forty thousand together. I'd keep taking two apprentices but send them to the college for a course on the machines as well. I'd ask Tom to show me the AI tools properly over Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A little like a change of minister at the chapel: you're not sure, but you give it a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've always been able to find apprentices a place. What happens if you can't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd keep them on a year longer myself, and pay for it. I've done that before when pig prices crashed. You don't take a young person on and then drop them because the market's gone funny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if jobs did shrink a lot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. That's progress, and it's brought us tractors and penicillin. But the people making the money from it should put something into training. That's not a handout, it's just decent.

S1.say: I'd say businesses that adapt will do well, as always. The college should teach young people to run the machines as well as the pigs, and the industry should train its own rather than ask government.
S1.think: It's fine for our farm, as we can buy what works. My worry is the apprentices, because if farms need fewer people I can't always ring a friend to find them a place.
S1.do: Watches for a year or two, then buys proven automatic feeders and camera weighing for about forty thousand. Keeps taking two apprentices and sends them on machine courses, and asks his son-in-law to teach him AI tools properly.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, like a new minister at chapel he's willing to give a chance.
S1.quote: You don't take a young person on and then drop them because the market's gone funny.
S1.fieldNote: He frames change as ordinary progress and wants industry, not government, to fund training. His concern is entirely for his apprentices, and he'd carry them himself if needed. His steady approach is to wait for bigger units to prove things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very quick. I'd want to read that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we don't know what this really means yet and we shouldn't panic. At chapel I'd say look after your neighbours and your family. I'd say the companies building these things owe the rest of us some honesty about what they're doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried for the apprentices, and for the pig price. We'll be all right, with the cottages and savings. But if a robot can do what I teach, I've two young people in the yard I can't promise a future, and that's never happened to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait the first six months before spending anything, because no one could know which machines worked. I'd hold the savings, not do the new farrowing house we'd planned for next year, about a hundred and fifty thousand. I'd keep both apprentices on to the end of their courses, whatever it cost, and talk to the college about what they should learn instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a bad diagnosis for someone you love, where you're fine but they might not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years' warning change for someone who likes to wait for proof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means waiting looks like doing nothing. Normally I let the big units try it, then I follow. In two years, they'd still be trying when it arrives. I'd be guessing, and I don't like guessing with other people's futures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the apprentices that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know, which is hard for me to say. Then I'd say finish your course, because knowing animals will count for something. And I'd say they can stay at Greystones till they've a plan. Helen would back me.

S2.say: I'd say we don't know what this means yet and shouldn't panic. I'd tell chapel to look after neighbours and family, and say the companies building it owe us honesty.
S2.think: We'll be fine with the cottages and savings, but I'd worry for the apprentices and the pig price. For the first time I'd have young people in the yard I couldn't promise a future.
S2.do: Waits six months before spending and shelves a planned hundred-and-fifty-thousand farrowing house. Keeps both apprentices to the end of their courses whatever it costs and asks the college what they should learn instead.
S2.feel: Anxious, like a bad diagnosis for someone he loves.
S2.quote: I'd be guessing, and I don't like guessing with other people's futures.
S2.fieldNote: Colin's anxiety is about duty to the young people he trains, not his own money. Two years breaks his habit of following proven units. He asks honesty from tech companies rather than help from government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like how things usually come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for the industry to get ready, if it's sensible. At the college board I'd push for courses on running and repairing farm robots, so the young ones have a trade. I'd say families should talk about it at the kitchen table, not leave it to the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's manageable for me. I'd be sixty-three when it lands, and I'd have seen the big units try things first. The question is Ben, actually, because building sites might go robotic too, and he's got men working for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the new farrowing house in year two but design it for robots, wider passages and charging points. I'd learn the AI tools properly with Tom's help, and get Stuart trained to run the place after me. I'd sit down with Ben and Helen and talk about the business and the cottages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I've a plan. Like a long, wet harvest, you just keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It brings back my old way: watch, then follow. And it gives the apprentices time to get a trade the machines need. In two years I'd be guessing, in five I'm deciding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools properly. At fifty-eight, is that hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Tom's patient, and I'm not as slow as I make out. I learnt to drive a combine with a computer in it at fifty. You just have to want to.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to get ready. I'd push the college board for robot maintenance courses and tell families to talk about it at the kitchen table.
S3.think: It's manageable for me, as I'd have seen bigger units try things first. My worry is my son, whose building firm might go robotic too.
S3.do: Builds the planned farrowing house in year two but designs it for robots. Learns AI tools with his son-in-law's help, trains his unit manager to take over and discusses the business and cottages with his son and wife.
S3.feel: Uneasy but with a plan, like a long wet harvest he keeps working through.
S3.quote: I learnt to drive a combine with a computer in it at fifty. You just have to want to.
S3.fieldNote: Five years restores his watch-then-follow habit and lets him plan the shed and succession. His worry shifts to his son's building firm. He is quietly more adaptable than he lets on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be retired. Sixty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse. To the apprentices I'd say learn the animals and learn the machines, and you'll do fine. I'd want the chapel to keep the community going while things change around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable. I'd hand over at sixty-five as I always planned, and Greystones would get its robots under Stuart. I'd miss the apprentices more than the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, buy machines when they're proven, keep taking apprentices till I retire. Around sixty-three I'd start handing the farm over to Stuart, maybe with a share. Helen and I would keep the cottages as our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like weather you can see coming over the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your grandchildren anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn a trade with their hands and to be honest, because people will still want to deal with someone they trust. That's what my grandfather said, and it's lasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd want to keep the same, whatever happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Harvest supper in the barn, for the staff and the chapel. We've done it every September for thirty years. Robots won't eat the sausage rolls, so we'll still need people for that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse. Apprentices should learn both the animals and the machines, and the chapel should hold the community together.
S4.think: It's comfortable for me: I'd hand over at sixty-five as planned and the farm would get robots under my unit manager. I'd miss the apprentices more than the work.
S4.do: Carries on, buying proven machines and taking apprentices until he retires. From about sixty-three hands the farm to his unit manager, perhaps with a share, while he and his wife live on the cottage income.
S4.feel: Calm, like weather he can see coming over the hill.
S4.quote: Robots won't eat the sausage rolls, so we'll still need people for that.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years falls after his planned retirement and he is calm. He'd hand the farm to his unit manager rather than to his children, who have their own careers. The harvest supper shows what he values: community over output.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of the apprentices. What would help is the companies making money from these machines paying into farm apprenticeships and courses. Not government cheques. Training, so young people have something to do with their hands and their heads.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the nine. Nine of my apprentices run farms now. If you want to know whether farming survives, ask them in ten years. I hope I'll have taught them well enough.

headlineQuote: If you want to know whether farming survives, ask them in ten years.
portrait: Colin Ito, 58, farms Greystones, a 250-sow pig unit with wheat and beans, with his wife Helen, who also runs their two holiday cottages. A chapel elder with traditional views, he has trained twenty-six apprentices and is proudest that nine now run farms. He adopts machines once bigger units prove them and uses AI tools occasionally with his son-in-law's help. Calm in the milder pictures, he becomes anxious in the two-year AGI picture, not for his money but because he couldn't promise his apprentices a future. With five or ten years he returns to his watch-then-follow habit, designs his new shed for robots and plans to hand over to his unit manager.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he couldn't promise a future to the apprentices he trains.
whatWouldHelp: Companies that profit from the machines paying for farm apprenticeships and courses, rather than government cheques.
